units.translation: a watch keeping watch in the open air

Thus from Hesychius, corrected as an interpolation, since in the best manuscript the reading is φρουρά πλέον κάουσα τῶν εἰρημένων [a watch burning more than the things mentioned]: about which see under προσαιθρίζω. After φλόγα [flame] Meineke Philol. vol. 20 p. 72. But elsewhere he wants the verse without the poet's name, preserved by Aelian V. H. 13, 1. άσσουσα (read διάττουσα, which Cobet corrected Mnem. 7 p. 224, unless he wrote ἄτ-τουσα) δ᾽ ἐξέλαμψεν ἀστραπῆς δίκην [and darting it flashed like lightning] he wants to insert, rejected by Wecklein in Ritschelii Museo Rhen. new series vol. 28 p. 696. It is without doubt another verse of the poet, spoken of Diana, as can be gathered from the words of Aelian
was the title of a play of Aeschylus fr. 23-31.
Ποντίων τε κυμά-των ἀνήριθμον [and of the countless sea waves]
Ποντίοις δάκεσι δὸς [give to the sea monsters]
Ὁ πόντιος ξεῖνος ἐκ πυρὸς συθεὶς θηκτὸς [the sea stranger, sharpened, rushing from fire]
Δμα-θέντες μεγάλως πλαγαῖσι [subdued greatly by blows]
Γῆθεν ἔκ τε [and from the earth]
and of the countless sea waves
the sea stranger, sharpened, rushing from fire
and the horse lord, ruler of the sea
Τραχεῖα πόντου Σαλ-μυδησία [rugged Salmydessian shore of the sea]
Κύμα δὲ πόντου τραχεῖ ῥοθίῳ [and a wave of the sea with rough surge]
Ξυντετάρακται δ᾽ αἰθὴρ [and the air is thrown into confusion]
Ζυγὸν ἀμφιβαλὼν αὐχένι [throwing the yoke around the neck]
Εὔτε πόντος ἐν μεσημ-βριναῖς κοίταις ἀκύμων νηνέμοις εὕδοι [when the sea sleeps in midday beds, waveless and windless]
Ἀλλόθρουν πόλιν [a city of foreign speech]
Ὑπέρ τε πόντον καὶ περιρρύτας [and over the sea and the sea-girt]
Ὑπέρ τε πόντον ἀπτέροις ποτήμασιν [and over the sea with wingless flights]
Ὧν πολὺς πόνος, πολὺς δὲ πόντος οἵνεκ᾽ ἠρόθη [for whose sake much toil and much sea was ploughed]
Δελφινοφόρον πόντου πεδίον [dolphin-bearing plain of the sea]
rugged Salmydessian shore of the sea
and a wave of the sea with rough surge
and the air is thrown into confusion
throwing the yoke around the neck
when the sea sleeps in midday beds, waveless and windless
and over the sea and the sea-girt
and over the sea with wingless flights
for whose sake much toil and much sea was ploughed
Ἰοὺ ἰοὺ πόπαξ, ἐπάθομεν, φίλαι, πάθος δυσ-αχές [Alas, alas, popax, we have suffered, friends, a grievous suffering]
An interjection nowhere else read nor mentioned by grammarians. Similar is πύππαξ [puppax].
